title: Demotion to expulsion
core: All four describe someone with authority moving a person (or thing) down or out against their will. The scale is *how far out you end up*: a worse seat at the same table, no seat, no throne, no country. They differ on what exactly gets taken — your rank, your office, or your right to be physically present — and on how high you had to be standing in the first place.

words.nuance: The only one where you're still **in** — you keep a place, just a demeaning one, and it names the destination (*to the bench, to a footnote*). It's also the only one that takes non-people: an idea, a dialect, a whole tradition can be **relegated** to irrelevance.

Takes the *role*, not the room — the ousted CEO still drives home; she just isn't CEO. Rank-neutral (board seat, throne, or shop lease) and method-neutral, which is why it's the newsroom default, and it almost always shows up passive: **ousted** by, never ousting oneself.

Same removal as *oust* but gated on altitude — reserved for rulers and high office, so a **deposed** manager reads as a joke or a sneer. Colder and more procedural than *overthrow*, and it carries a second, unrelated legal sense: to take sworn out-of-court testimony.

The one about geography, not rank — you're put outside a place and forbidden to return, by explicit decree. Old and absolute in flavour, which is what lets it go figurative on the intangible (**banish** the thought, the fear, the smell) where the others can't.

exam_note: Watch the two traps: *relegate* looks like removal but only ever means demotion-in-place, and *depose* fails whenever the subject isn't a ruler — or is secretly the courtroom sense.
